title: ‘This is the guy.’ The legacy of World Trade Center designer Minoru Yamasaki
text:
The World Trade Center Twin Towers were a focal point of the attacks of Sept. 11. The buildings were envisioned by architect Minoru Yamasaki, who was born and raised in Seattle. Journalist Knute “Mossback” Berger is an editor-at-large at Cascade PBS, and host of “Mossback's Northwest.” He told KUOW’s Kim Malcolm about his research into Yamasaki's life and legacy.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Kim Malcolm: This anniversary of the attacks stirs up so much memory and emotion for so many of us. To see the Twin Towers fall 25 years ago and witness the aftermath was just heartbreaking. What do we know about Yamasaki’s vision for these iconic buildings?

Knute Berger: Well, he got the job of designing the Twin Towers because of the iconic building he built for the Seattle World's Fair, which was then the Federal Science Pavilion. We know it as the Pacific Science Center now. But he had a long track record throughout the 40s, 50s, 60s of building very beautiful, very serene and inspiring projects. This inspired the New York and New Jersey Port Authority to hire him to do this ambitious project of building what would be the tallest buildings in the world.

This was atypical for the kind of thing he'd been designing, but they had come to the World's Fair, and had seen the science pavilion. They'd seen the public's response. Here was modern architecture people could love! And so they decided, this is the guy.

How did he deal with these clients? It was such a big project.

I think part of the issue was the project was technically challenging. It had all kinds of issues in terms of what kind of structure it was going to be, how much floor space would be rentable to commercial clients, and would these buildings stand up? Would they sway too much in the wind? It's huge.

His aesthetic was, "I'm going to make these slim. I'm going to make them elegant. I'm going to make them inspirational. I want people to look at these towers and think, ‘These are beautiful.’"

You wrote a piece a few years ago for the 9/11 anniversary. You wrote that perhaps the best that could be said about the design and the engineering of the Twin Towers is that quite a few people in the buildings were able to escape on Sept. 11. Can you say more about that?

Unlike buildings with lots of pillars in the middle holding them up, the Twin Towers had their structural frame on the exterior. That’s been credited with saving thousands of lives in the event, because when the planes hit the towers, they didn't collapse immediately. People who've looked into that have said probably 3,000 to 4,000 lives were saved just by his design.

Knute, Minoru Yamasaki never saw what happened to the Twin Towers. He died in 1986. And those towers were undoubtedly Yamasaki’s highest profile project. How do you think about his legacy?

I think of his legacy as that of an extremely creative and sensitive person, somebody who really believed that those towers would come to represent democracy and aspirational future.

I don't think it ever would've occurred to him that they would become targets of hate. What happened was shocking to all of us, but I think it would've shocked him deeply because that was not what he poured into that or any of his projects. It was the antithesis of what he believed he was trying to do.
